title.en: Cat-kin and the Five Gems of the Korean Character

region.en: Island of Gems in the sapphire sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 海上寶石之島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Etiological fairy tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Cat-kin and the Queen Mother', eBook #67180

summary.en: Farmer Pak of Nai-po prays for a daughter and plucks a pussy willow the same day she is born: they name her Cat-kin, Little Puss. Sitting under a persimmon tree she calls the earth-spirit — the air fills with sweet perfume, and before her stands the Western Queen Mother in a blue-jade chariot with golden wheels drawn by milk-white horses. Taken up through the clouds, Cat-kin looks down on her father's village, a grey mass of thatched roofs, and beholds an island in the center of the sapphire sea: the trees are emeralds, the roofs gold, the windows diamonds. On the Island of Gems the Queen presents her to the court and bestows five gems — jade, crystal, malachite, amber and agate — sent back to the capital to be made a princess and wed to the king's son. By lot the caskets are drawn by nobles, and in them the Korean people receive their national traits: Procrastination (putting off until tomorrow what ought to be done today), Hospitality (entertaining friends and strangers even to the making of one's self poor), Inexactness (not thinking clearly, counting correctly or stating facts precisely — when telling a story, 'blowing a conch'), Love of family, and Sense of humor. Just as five fingers make up the hand, so the average Koreans are known by the five traits, for better or for worse.
summary.zh: 農夫朴氏祈女，得桂心。一日呼地靈，西王母乘碧玉車而至，攜之登寶石之島——樹皆翡翠，屋頂黃金，窗為鑽石。母后以玉、水晶、孔雀石、琥珀、瑪瑙五寶賜之，遣其還都為公主。王子貴戚抽籤分寶匣，遂得國人之五性：遲緩（今日之事拖至明日）、好客（待客至貧而不悔）、不確（言事多誇，曰『吹螺』）、愛家、幽默。五指成拳，五性成人，朝鮮民族之性盡在其中。

sensitivity.note: Fairy etiology of national character traits written by a Western observer; interpretive generalizations recorded as story, not ethnography.

passages.text: One day, sitting under a persimmon tree and reading a story, Cat-kin held the book in one hand, while she struck the ground several times, saying earnestly, 'Earth-spirit, earth-spirit, come to me; come up and see me.' All of a sudden the air seemed heavy with sweet perfume, and a silver mist like a cloud spread over her house and garden. Then a dazzling light flooded everything and there stood before her a glistening chariot made of blue jade with golden wheels, drawn by milk-white horses, and on a seat of shining silver sat the Western Heavenly Queen Mother herself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Cat-kin and the Queen Mother' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Come forward, little maid, fear not. I shall take you with me to my palace, in the Island of Gems, and give you all you want, besides showering blessings on your people, if you will come.' Cat-kin came boldly forward and knelt at the base of the chariot; the Mother Queen touched her with her milk-white jade wand carved like a lotus bud, and made the little girl rise. Up through and far above the clouds the host of bright beings flew, and Cat-kin was told to look over the side of the chariot: the whole village looked only like a grey mass of thatched roofs, and in the center of the azure sea was an island where the trees were emeralds, the roofs of the houses gold, and the windows diamonds, so full of light that no lamps were necessary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Cat-kin and the Queen Mother' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her Majesty's chamberlain read the proclamation, which declared that the Queen looked with great favor upon the Korean people, and had decided to bestow great gifts upon them through this, their daughter, with five precious traits of disposition and character: jade, crystal, malachite, amber and agate. Cat-kin would be sent back to the King's palace in the capital of her home land and made a princess, to marry none but the king's son. One by one the caskets were opened by each prince, and therein he discovered a trait in the character of the Korean people: Procrastination, Hospitality, Inexactness ('blowing a conch,' that is, exaggerating), Love of family, and Sense of humor. And what the Queen Mother predicted came true: just as five fingers make up the hand, so the average people among the Koreans are known by the five traits, for better or for worse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Cat-kin and the Queen Mother' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Magic Peach and the Thousand-Year Wandering

region.zh: 海上寶石之島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Fairy tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Magic Peach', eBook #67180

summary.en: On an island so far away that no ship ever sailed there stands the seven-storied palace of Su Wang Moo, the Western Queen Mother, always ready to help good mortals; her gardens grow the celestial peach of longevity, served on little golden tables, whose juice makes an old person's body new so that one who eats will live hundreds of years — and none can get any unless the Queen herself gives them, the trees jealously guarded by genii and dragons. Hearing of the virtues of a certain king's son, she sends a palace maiden in a dragon chariot to invite him; his mother warns him against the sirens, and the Queen warns the maiden not to let the prince fall in love with her, or she will be disgraced and die early. At the feast the prince eats the peach of longevity — each morsel making him feel as if he were gaining a century of vigor — and forgets himself, tossing a peach to the kneeling maid, who breaks the rule of the palace and catches it, bites into it and swallows the morsel. A golden mist falls; the Korean story-teller stops his booth in a back street of Seoul to take up a collection. More than a thousand years afterwards, a hermit of the Ever White range — honored almost as a worshiped sage, before whom even tigers and leopards forget they have claws — meets a woman of unwrinkled, rosy face in the dress of ages gone: the same palace maid, banished for a thousand years, wandering the nine provinces for the prince who tossed her the peach. His beard falls off, black hair covers his bald head, and he becomes young again; a news-gathering dragon tells the Queen, a golden chariot bears both to the Island of Gems, and there the Queen orders them to be married.
summary.zh: 西王母居海上仙島，園中蟠桃能延壽千載，非母后親賜不可得。王后遣仙女召王子赴宴。王子食蟠桃，覺每口增壽百年，忘形以桃擲侍女；侍女破宮規而接而食之。金霧忽起，說書人收錢。千餘年後，白山中有老仙，猛獸不敢近；遇一衣古服之少艾，自認即當年侍女，為此桃被謫千年，遍遊九道以求其人。仙翁鬚落髮生，返老還童。青龍報於王母，金車來迎，遂成婚於寶石之島。

sensitivity.note: Queen Mother of the West (Xiwangmu) lore shared across East Asia; tagged as East Asian heritage.

passages.text: Now in the gardens of the Queen's Palace, on the Island of Gems, there grow wonderful fruits of a rich, ripe color, brilliant with light and sheen. These, when served at the banquets and eaten, have the power of making the guest live very long, even for thousands of years. Especially powerful is the celestial peach of longevity, which is served on little golden tables, its juice makes an old person's body new, so that one who eats the peach will live hundreds of years. None, even of the Queen's servants, or her waiting maids, or any of the genii or dragons, can bestow the peach of longevity on mortals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Peach' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: It happened that the Queen, hearing of the virtues of a certain king's son, despatched one of her lovely maidens, in one of her ten thousand dragon chariots, inviting him to visit Her Majesty. His anxious mother warned him against looking too long at the lovely princesses, fearing that beneath their rosy faces they were really sirens, possibly even sea monsters in female form, and might eat him up. On the other hand the Queen of the Island of Gems warned the maiden to beware lest the prince fall in love with her: 'Don't trust a pigeon to carry grain.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Peach' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Towards the end of the feast, feeling in a jolly mood, the prince picked up one of the peaches and pared and sliced it, greatly enjoying its juicy nectar. Every morsel of the pulp made him feel as if he were gaining a century of vigor. Yet every moment the maiden kneeling near him seemed to grow more charming — the change was in him, not in her. So intoxicated was the prince that he picked out one of the finest-looking peaches and tossed it over to the pretty maiden; and the maid of honor, so wrapped up in admiration of the princely guest, broke the rule of the Palace of Gems: she threw out her hands and caught the peach deftly, and to the horror of all who saw her bit into it and swallowed the morsel. What it was that happened the very next moment even the fairies could not tell, for a golden mist seemed to fall in the banquet hall, enveloping everything.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Peach' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: More than a thousand years afterwards it was known that in the high mountains of the Ever White range lived a holy hermit, honored almost as worshiped by the people; even the wild beasts appeared tame in his presence. One day on his walks he met a woman of fair countenance, whose dress betokened ages gone. She was the same palace maid who in the Western Queen Mother's palace had waited upon him, once a gay prince and now the holy hermit; for catching and eating the peach which the princely guest had tossed to her, the Queen had ordered her banishment for a thousand years. During all this time she had been seeking the prince, for she knew that neither she nor he could die till the thousand years had passed; not finding him, she went back to the Island of Gems and humbly begged the Queen to extend her term of life. Now, having met the holy hermit, she was happy, for she could see his soul. The hermit's long white beard fell off, his bald head was covered with luxuriant black hair, and he became young again; and already by a flying dragon, famous for gathering news from all parts of the universe, the Queen had been told of the meeting of the lovers. A golden chariot drawn by two dragons bore them swiftly to the Island of Gems, where the Queen ordered them to be married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Peach' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Stone Fire Eater before the Palace Gate

region.en: Volcano southwest of Seoul; palace gate (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城西南火山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Etiological fairy tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Great Stone Fire Eater', eBook #67180

summary.en: Ages ago a great Fire Spirit lived inside a mountain southwest of Seoul, always hungry, devouring trees and forests, stones and rocks, throwing the hard stuff out of his mouth in the form of lava; he spent his time in a volcano, and nothing tasted so good as things men built — an especial titbit was the royal palace. He waits for his friend the South Wind, and by night with her prancing gusts he swallows the palace, leaving only a level waste of ashes. The wise men of the king import a big Chinese dragon, decorated with amber beads and a horsehair hat, to guard the swamp — but the petted dragon makes it rain too often, grows sulky, and falls asleep one night while the winds are out on a dance, and the Fire Imp swallows the palace again. Then the well-diggers dig a big pond in the monster's path, chilling him nearly out; and the master stone-cutter is at last commissioned to chisel out of a mighty block of white granite a beast that could eat flames and be ugly enough to scare the Fire Imp — fire-proof scales like a salamander, curly hair like asbestos, a mouth full of big fangs, half alligator and half water-tortoise. One sight of the hideous stony monster is enough: by his freezing glance alone the Great Flame Eater frightens away the Fire Imp forever, and the royal palace is not once burned again. To-day the ugly brute still keeps watch before the palace gate.
summary.zh: 漢城西南火山中有火魔，恆飢，能吞木石，吐為熔巖。嘗與南風合謀，一夜盡焚王宮。王聘中國巨龍鎮之，龍驕惰失職，宮再焚。乃鑿大池以阻之，火魔過池而凍。復命石匠以白玉鑿神獸：鱗如火蜥，毛如石棉，口有利齒，似鼉非鼉。火魔一見，寒心而遁，終身不敢近。今宮門前石獸猶在，即其物也。

sensitivity.note: Origin tale of the haetae/xiezhi guardian statues at Gwanghwamun; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Ages ago there lived a great Fire Spirit inside of a mountain to the southwest of Seoul. He was always hungry, and his food was anything that would burn: he devoured trees, forests, dry grass, wood, and whatever he could get hold of; when those were not within his reach, he ate stones and rocks, and threw the hard stuff out of his mouth in the form of lava. Nothing tasted so good to the Fire Eater as things which men built, such as houses, stables, fences, and general property. An especial titbit, that he longed to swallow, was the royal palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Great Stone Fire Eater' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Let me know when you're ready,' said the Fire Spirit to the South Wind, 'and we'll have a splendid blaze.' When the sun went down and it was dark, the Fire Spirit climbed out of his rocky home in the volcano and strode toward Seoul, the South Wind prancing and capering with him until the streets of the capital were so gusty that no one with a wide-brimmed hat dared go outdoors. By the time the sun did rise there was nothing but a level waste of ashes where the large buildings had been.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Great Stone Fire Eater' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At tremendous cost and trouble one of China's biggest dragons, capable of making rain and of spouting tons of water on its enemies, was shipped over and kept in a swamp, honored with a royal decoration, a string of amber beads over its ear, a horsehair hat, a nobleman's girdle, and all the turnips it desired to eat. But it was all in vain: the petted dragon made it rain too often, then grew sulky and neglected its duty, and finally became fat and lazy and one night fell asleep when it ought to have been on guard, for the winds were out on a dance. The Fire Imp leaped out of its volcano prison, rode quickly on the South Wind to Seoul, and in a few hours had again swallowed the royal palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Great Stone Fire Eater' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The master stone-cutter was invited to chisel out the figure of a beast that could eat flames and be ugly enough to scare away the Fire Imp. Out of the heart of the mountains a mighty block of white granite was brought to Seoul on rollers by thousands of laborers, and hidden behind canvas the workmen toiled until the Great Stone Flame Eater was ready to take his permanent seat in front of the palace gate. One night the Fire Imp crept out and moved toward the city; one sight of the hideous stony monster was enough — enormous fire-proof scales like a salamander, curly hair like asbestos, its mouth full of big fangs, half alligator and half water-tortoise. So by his freezing glance alone the Great Flame Eater frightened away the Fire Imp, so that he never came again and the royal palace was not once burned. To-day the ugly brute still keeps watch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Great Stone Fire Eater' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Pigling and the Pigeons, the Cow and Tokgabi

region.en: Magistrate's house and royal festival (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 官宅與都會慶典（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Cinderella-type tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Pigling and Her Proud Sister', eBook #67180

summary.en: Pear Blossom, suddenly motherless, is hated by the proud widow her father marries and by her daughter Violet, who call her Pigling and make her clean the rice, cook and attend the fire. When a great festival comes, the stepmother sets before her a huge straw bag of unhulled rice and a big cracked water jar: hull all the rice and fill the crock to the brim before she dares go out. A flock of pigeons comes down and husks the rice with beak and claw; out of the fire hole crawls the sooty imp Tokgabi, who stops up the crack with clay and pours a dozen buckets into the crock. At the picnic task of weeding the garden, a huge black cow beams compassion from its great liquid eyes, eats up the weeds and clears the walk; following it into the woods, Pigling finds the most delicious fruit. The jealous stepsister tries to counterfeit the miracle — stays home to see the cow — and is led into a swamp, thorns tearing her clothes till she gets home in rags with her beauty gone. Rosy and round, Pigling is won by a young gentleman from the south through a go-between, and grand is the wedding: to this day in her boudoir stands an earthen figure of a black cow, while the pigeons hover about a pear tree that sheds a snowy shower of fragrant petals every spring.
summary.zh: 梨花喪母，繼母與妹虐之，呼曰『小豬』。慶日令其脫米三斗、注破甕之水滿，乃許出門。群鴿下而啄米自淨；灶中托孤鬼出，以泥補甕，汲水注滿而去。又令鋤園草，則黑牛至，盡食其草，犁平其徑，引之入林得美果。妒妹效之，反為牛引至沼澤，刺荊破衣，容毀而歸。梨花卒為南來貴公子所聘，婚禮極盛。至今其妝閣中猶供陶牛，而鴿群每歲繞其梨樹。

sensitivity.note: Korean Cinderella (Kongjwi-Patchwi type); no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Pear Blossom had been the name of a little Korean maid who was suddenly left motherless. When her father, Kang Wa, a magistrate high in office, married again, he took for his wife a proud widow whose daughter was named Violet. Mother and daughter hated housework and made Pear Blossom clean the rice, cook the food and attend to the fire; besides never speaking a kind word, they called her Pigling, or Little Pig, which made the girl weep often.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Pigling and Her Proud Sister' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was to be a great festival in the city. Poor Pigling wanted very much to have a look at the pageant, but the cruel stepmother, setting before her a huge straw bag of unhulled rice and a big cracked water jar, told her she must husk all the rice and fill the crock to the brim before she dared to go out. She heard a whir and a rush of wings and down came a flock of pigeons, who first lighted on her head and shoulders, and then, hopping to the floor, diligently with beak and claw made the rice lie in a heap, clean, white and glistening. There crawled out of the fire hole a sooty black imp, named Tokgabi: 'Don't cry, I'll mend the broken part and fill the big jar for you' — and he stopped up the crack with clay and poured a dozen buckets of water from the well into the crock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Pigling and Her Proud Sister' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next time, the stepmother told Pigling she must not go out until she had hoed all the weeds out of the garden and pulled up all the grass between the stones of the walk. While weeping, a huge black cow came along, and out of its great liquid eyes seemed to beam compassion upon the kitchen slave; in ten mouthfuls the animal ate up the weeds, and, between its hoof and lips, soon made an end of the grass in the stone pathway. With her tears dried Pigling followed the brute out over the meadows into the woods, where she found the most delicious fruit her eyes ever rested upon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Pigling and Her Proud Sister' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the jealous stepsister heard of the astonishing doings of the black cow, she stayed home on the next gala-day to enjoy a feast in the forest also; but the animal took it into its head to go very fast, and into unpleasant places, till the girl found herself in a swamp, wet, miry and full of brambles, the thorny bushes tearing her clothes and scratching her face, so that when she got home she was in rags and her beauty was gone. But Pigling, rosy and round, looked so lovely that a young man from the south, of good family and visiting the capital, was struck with her beauty; grand was the wedding, and to this day in the boudoir of Pear Blossom there stands an earthen figure of a black cow moulded from the clay of her home province, while the pigeons hover about a pear tree that bursts into bloom every spring time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Pigling and Her Proud Sister' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mirror That Made Trouble in Cucumberville

region.en: Village north of Seoul; magistrate's court (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Comic folk tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Mirror That Made Trouble', eBook #67180

summary.en: Miller Kim of Cucumberville walks to Seoul with his savings, buys gifts for wife and daughters — and, cheated by a shop clerk into thinking he'll see fairies, buys a metal disc in which he sees a man's face that laughs when he laughs and vanishes when he dodges. Home, the girls open the mirror case: the mother sees a young woman — 'Your father has brought home another woman, a ge-sang, from Seoul, to take my place'; the daughter sees a tyrant; the grandmother an old woman; grandfather an unfilial second father; and the wife, dragging her husband by the topknot to the judge, charges him with every crime — all she can prove is that he brought something round made of metal, as full of evil magic as Tokgabi. The judge himself, holding the mirror, sees a man in official robes with a string of twenty-eight amber beads and a silver stork, and chokes with rage that another magistrate should come to take his place. At the height of the hullaballoo the royal inspector arrives from the capital, who, accustomed to the comforts of the great city, explains what a mirror is, scolds them for their folly, and counsels: whenever angry or jealous, pull the tops off five turnips, or drink slowly a cup of rice water before speaking an angry word. Thereafter nearly every one who could afford it bought a mirror, and the mirror-makers of Seoul grew rich.
summary.zh: 磨坊主金某至漢京購鏡歸。母見鏡中有婦，怒曰『夫攜妓歸矣』；女曰『繼母也』；婆曰『老嫗也』；翁曰『不孝之子再進一翁，誰給他飯吃』；妻曳夫之髻告官，謂其攜妖物以亂家。縣令自照鏡，見冠服儼然、耳懸琥珀珠之官人，大怒，以為新官至而奪其缺。適欽差至，笑而釋之，曰『此鏡也，照者見己面耳。怒時拔五蘿蔔頭，或徐飲米湯一口，則怒氣自消』。村人自是爭購鏡，漢京鏡匠驟富。

sensitivity.note: Comic tale; parallel to korean-looking-glass-prodigies (Griffis Hermit Nation version).

passages.text: In a village up north, which in English we should call Cucumberville, lived a miller, Mr. Kim and his wife Cho. One fine May morning he started off to walk to Seoul and see the sights. While in the silk shop the clerk saw that Kim was from the country and thought he would have a little fun, telling him about the fairies and pointing out a shop across the way, where, if he looked at the round thing, he would see and feel as he never felt or saw before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Mirror That Made Trouble' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: There he stood in front of a round thing like the moon, in which was a man's face. When Kim laughed the fellow laughed too; when he made a wry face, the other person did the same; no matter how quickly Kim might turn around to catch him, he was gone. Kim had never before seen a mirror and did not know what it might be; yet thinking it was almost like fairy magic, he bought the metal disc and took it back with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Mirror That Made Trouble' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: No sooner had the girls opened the mirror case than terrible things happened. The mother saw the face of a young woman and instantly broke out in a fit of jealous passion: 'Your father has brought home another woman, a ge-sang, from Seoul, to take my place.' The daughter cried out that she would be a tyrant; the grandmother would not have this old woman in the house; the grandfather turned almost purple with rage — 'is my son so unfilial as to bring another old man into the house? How can he support two fathers?' The wife, seizing her husband by his topknot, dragged him to the house of the judge and charged him with all the crimes known in the codes; yet all she could prove was that he had brought something round, made of metal, as full of evil magic as Tokgabi and all his imps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Mirror That Made Trouble' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the judge held up the mirror before his eyes he suddenly became like a demon in his rage: on the face of the round thing he saw a man in official robes, with a high round hat, a string of twenty-eight big round amber beads, the embroidered breastpiece, and the little silver stork that held together the folds of a judge's coat of office. All this made him almost choke with anger, at the idea that another magistrate should come into the village of Cucumberville to take his place. Just then a messenger announced the royal inspector direct from the king, who explained what a mirror was, gave them all a mild scolding for their folly, and counseled that whenever they felt angry or jealous, to pull the tops off five turnips, or drink slowly a cup of rice water before speaking an angry word. After that, nearly every one who could afford it bought a mirror, and the mirror-makers of Seoul slapped their thighs for joy and grew rich.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Mirror That Made Trouble' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Old Timber Top Turned into a Bull

region.en: Butcher's inn on the Seoul road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赴京道客舍（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Transformation fairy tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Old Timber Top', eBook #67180

summary.en: Old Timber Top, a rich and stingy lumber dealer who would skin a mosquito for his hide and tallow, buys up even the splendid trees planted around poor families' ancestors' graves, leaving only the sawdust — and sets out for Seoul to win office through a relative, fawning like a slave while despised even by the servants. His fortune shrinks in gifts to his patron; his wife sells their house; the wine-shop wits debate whether, if his skull were opened, pumpkin seeds or timber would be found inside it. Bankrupt, on the road home he shelters at the inn of a butcher's wife, and waking hears the butcher ask where the ox is that he must sell on market day: four fairy sticks under his back, horns grow out of his head, his lips thicken like sausages, a tail sprouts, and the ring is slipped through his nose. Sold and tied to a turnip field's wall while the drover drinks, he eats the turnips roots and all — presto, the horns shrink, the ring crashes down, and Old Timber Top is a man again. He steals back the four fairy sticks, taps his rich Seoul relative with them — half man, half ox with horns and hoofs — while mudangs drum and dance and doctors needle and moxa in vain; then returns as the world's greatest physician with a sauce of pounded turnip, one spoonful restoring the man entirely. He becomes physician to the king, lives to a good old age with seventeen grandchildren — and the fairies claim they did it all.
summary.zh: 木頭翁者，吝嗇木商也，兼伐墓樹，人皆惡之。入京十年無所成，貧而歸。夜宿屠夫之妻逆旅，被仙杖一擊，頭生角，唇如臘，尾自出，鼻貫環，化為牛，繫於蘿蔔田。其人啖蘿蔔，角縮環落，復為人。乃竊仙杖歸，潛擊其京中富親，親遂半人半牛。巫醫束手。翁自言有秘藥，搗蘿蔔為醬，一匙而人形頓復。翁由是為御醫，壽至耄耋，孫十七人。仙家自誇其功。

sensitivity.note: Transformation-and-cure comic tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: This driver was a rich and stingy fellow who had made a fortune in lumber. He used to buy up all the trees he could. It is the custom in Korea to plant the most beautiful trees around tombs or in the cemeteries; when this skin-flint heard of a family which had become so poor that they must sell the splendid trees which had been planted around their ancestors' graves, he sent his agents to buy the timber, chop down and saw up the grand trees, leaving only the sawdust on the graves, while the people wept to lose what they loved. In this way the landscape was spoiled, for the Koreans love natural scenery and almost worship fine trees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old Timber Top' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: On his way back, a big storm came on and he begged for shelter over night at the inn kept by the wife of a butcher. He was so tired that he kept on sleeping till very late. Waking up from one of his naps, he heard what he thought was the big butcher asking in a gruff tone, 'Where is that ox? I must sell him this morning, for it is market day.' In less than a minute more, the man and his wife entered the room with four sticks which the fairies had put there, a halter and rope, and an iron ring: thrusting the stick under Old Timber Top's back, in a moment he felt horns growing out of his head and his lips becoming thick as sausages; a tail sprouted at his other end and the four sticks became four legs, and the butcher was slipping the ring through his nose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old Timber Top' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The new owner tied Timber Top's nose to the low wall which enclosed a turnip field, and went inside a wine shop; while the drover's wine went in, his wits went out. Meanwhile Timber Top looked over the low wall, and, yielding to temptation, pulled up with his teeth some of the plants by the roots, chewing the green leaves and grinding the turnips and swallowing them. Presto! The horns drew in and shrivelled up. The ring dropped out of his nose and fell with a crash on the stones of the village path; his two forelegs turned into arms and Old Timber Top was a man, and himself once again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old Timber Top' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He returned hastily to the inn and stole the butcher's four fairy sticks, then hied over the roads toward the capital. Reaching Seoul, he went to the house of his rich relative, and going into his host's bedroom, tapped the high lord of the house with the fairy sticks: forthwith the man's head became horns at the top, with muzzle of thick lips in front, his hands turned into front hoofs and his legs into the hind quarters of a bull, half animal and half man. The mudangs with drums and dancing and songs kept up such a terrible racket, and the doctors kept on with their awful medicines, rubbing, pounding, sticking needles and burning moxa — yet not a hoof or horn changed. Then Old Timber Top appeared, bought a fine large turnip, pounded it into a sauce, and put a spoonful on the big tongue: at once the horns shortened until they disappeared, the lips thinned, and in the wagging of a dog's tail the mighty man of the house had become himself again. Old Timber Top set up a medicine office, practiced among the nobility and became physician to the king, yet all the time the fairies claimed that they did it all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old Timber Top' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Sir One Long Body and Madam Thousand Feet

region.en: Under a stone by a persimmon tree (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Comic animal tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Sir One Long Body and Madam Thousand Feet', eBook #67180

summary.en: Under an old stone below a persimmon tree lives Miss Thousand Feet of the famous Pil family, lead-colored, modest, curling into a ball if stepped on; in another village lives rich, promising Mr. Long Body of the Wum family, whose business is to eat his way through the ground. Through the proper go-between the six proprieties are completed and the engagement announced — and the gossips break out on both sides: he would never pay his shoemaker for a thousand feet; she would be a slave making, washing and starching his one-legged trousers. Miss Pil broods over the long coats to come, refuses to prepare her trousseau, and writes to break off; Mr. Wum, figuring what five hundred pairs of shoes would cost, sees himself ruined and writes first, begging her to secure another husband. The letters cross on the road; each has a refusal before the ink is dry, so neither can complain. To this day Miss Pil remains single and Mr. Wum has no wife: she still goes shoeless, hiding from light under a stone, and he keeps out of sight underground, for he has nothing to wear.
summary.zh: 柿樹石下有千足娘子（畢氏），蚯蚓郎君（嚴氏）遣媒通好。兩村閒話頓起：或曰『千足之鞋，何由措辦』；或曰『一褲如蛇，漿洗何其勞』。女愁而悔婚，修書往絕；郎算鞋價五百雙，亦修書請退。兩書交錯於道，墨未乾而各得絕音，故兩不相怨。至今千足者無履而匿於石下，蚓者無衣而遁於土中。

sensitivity.note: Comic courtship tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There once lived under an old stone below a persimmon tree a fair young creature named Miss Thousand Feet. She wore lead-colored clothes and had so many toes to take care of that any one who tried to count them soon got tired and called the whole amount a thousand. She was very modest, and if any one stepped on her toes she curled up, first into a ring and then into a ball, so that men called her a pill millipede, for she belonged to the Pil family, one of the most famous in all Korea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Sir One Long Body and Madam Thousand Feet' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In another village lived a rich, fat, young and promising male creature, named Mr. Long Body, of the Wum family, whose business was to eat his way through the ground. He sent letters and opened the business through a go-between, until the six proprieties had been completed and the engagement of Mr. Wum and Miss Pil was announced. What a clatter of gossip was at once heard in both villages! No one ever thought that such a handsome fellow as Mr. Long Body Wum would ever marry into the Pil family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Sir One Long Body and Madam Thousand Feet' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Miss Pil brooded over the awfully long coats and one-legged trousers she would be obliged to sit up at nights to make, wash, starch and gloss; she refused to prepare her own trousseau, and decided to write a letter telling him she felt unable to hold to the marriage engagement. But before she had dropped the water on the ink stone, Mr. Long Body had got wind of her complaining, and began to doubt whether he could buy shoes enough to fit all the feet of his betrothed: at the sight of five hundred pairs of shoes his breath almost failed him and he saw himself ruined. The substance of what he wrote was that, owing to his small fortune, he could not think of asking her to share his poverty, but begged her to secure another husband. Now it happened that the letters crossed on the road; each had a refusal before the ink was dry, so neither could complain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Sir One Long Body and Madam Thousand Feet' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

texts.period: Chilseok (seventh night of the seventh moon) star myth from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Sky Bridge of Birds', eBook #67180

summary.en: No bird is more common in Korea than the magpie — except on the seventh day of the seventh month, when every well-bred magpie is far up in the sky building a bridge across the River of Stars, with their wings for the cables and their heads to form the floor, a pathway for lovers on either side of the Silver Stream; any lazy bird found about the houses that day is pelted by every dirty-faced brat. The proof that the bridge was walked over is the bare heads of the magpies, their feathers worn off by the tramping of the crowd of retainers who follow the Prince of Star Land across the bridge to meet his bride. In the Kingdom of the Stars a king had a lovely daughter, skilful weaver and model of all diligence; the handsome prince who married her gave himself up to waste and gambling until, degraded to his last string of cash, the king banished him six months' distance to the north side of the River of Heaven and exiled the princess as far to the south — ordaining, as a proof of compassion, that on the seventh night of the seventh moon they might meet for a few hours. When their tears flood the Starry River and threaten to float away houses and people, millions of magpies assemble in the air: they put their heads together to furnish a floor so closely that the bridge looks paved with white granite, and with their pinions hold up the great arch over which the prince crosses to his bride with all his baggage and train.
summary.zh: 韓人最敬鵲。七月七日，羣鵲皆上天河，以翼為索、以首為橋面，架橋於銀漢之上，使牽牛織女得會。是日見鵲者，童子必擊之。橋成之證，則鵲頂皆禿——為帝從踐踏故也。織女勤織，牛郎蕩產博戲，天帝乃謫之：一在河東，一在河西，歲許一會。二人相對而泣，淚落成洪流，幾沒人間。萬鵲銜翼為橋，白如砥石，帝乃攜從渡橋而會。

sensitivity.note: Chilseok star-bridge myth; parallels the Qixi/Tanabata cluster and record korean-chingyuh-kyainoo-star-lovers.

passages.text: No bird is more common in Korea than the magpie. Every day in the year, except the seventh day of the seventh month, the air is full of them. On that date they have a standing engagement every year: every well-bred magpie is then far up in the sky building a bridge across the River of Stars, called the Milky Way. With their wings for the cables, and their heads to form the floor of the bridge, they make a pathway for lovers on either side of the Silver Stream. If a single one be found about the houses on the seventh of August, every dirty-faced brat throws sticks or stones at the poor creature for not being about its business of bridge-building.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sky Bridge of Birds' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: To prove beyond a doubt that the bridge was made and walked over, you have only to look at the bare heads of the magpies at this time: their feathers have been entirely worn off by the tramping of the crowd of retainers who follow the Prince of Star Land across the bridge to meet his bride. If it be wet weather on the morning of this day of the Weaver Maiden and the Cattle Prince, the rain-drops are the tears of joy shed by the lovers at their first meeting; if showers fall in the afternoon, they are the tears of sadness at saying farewell; if any thunder is heard, it comes from the rumble of the wagons which carry the baggage of the prince and princess as they move away, each from the other, homeward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sky Bridge of Birds' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Long, long ago, in the Kingdom of the Stars, a king reigned who had a lovely daughter, a skilful weaver, a model of all diligence. A young and very handsome prince came to her father's court and fell in love with the pretty princess, and the wedding was celebrated with great splendor. But the prince, instead of following his bride's good example, gave himself up to waste and extravagance: he wasted his own fortune and his wife's dowry, sold all his oxen and calves to get money only to lose it in gambling, until he was so scandalously poor, being on his last string of cash, that he was in danger of being degraded from his rank as prince.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sky Bridge of Birds' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King of the Stars banished the prince far away, six months' distance from the north side of the River of Heaven, and exiled the princess a half year's measure of space from the south side of the Starry Stream; yet, as a signal proof of his compassion, he ordained that on one night of the year, on the seventh night of the seventh moon, they might meet for a few hours. Feeling that the great gulf of space could not be spanned, the loving couple burst into tears, the flood deluging the earth below. The four-footed creatures, fish and fowls held a convention, and the magpies resolved to help: millions assembled in the air and began, under the direction of their wisest chiefs, to make with a mass of wings a flying bridge from shore to shore of the Starry Stream, putting their heads together to furnish a floor so closely that the bridge looked as if it were paved with white granite. Every year for ages past, on the seventh day of the seventh month, the magpies have done this.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sky Bridge of Birds' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Longka and the Rock of the Falling Flower

region.en: Cliff House above the river, southern Korea (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Imjin War legend from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913); the rock's story dates to the Japanese invasion (c. 1597)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Longka, the Dancing Girl', eBook #67180

summary.en: When the islanders' great army marches to the capital, a clever Korean admiral has invented an iron-clad ship that rams and sinks their war junks; before they leave, they smash statues and monuments, take marble pagodas apart to load on their ships, and entice or force away hundreds of Korean potters, artists and craftsmen. In a town of southern Korea lived a beautiful dancing girl named Longka, taken prisoner and made a waitress in the general's tent. At a great banquet in the Cliff House, illuminated with a thousand wax lights, the pretty dancer robed in pure white performs the story-telling Korean dances — of birds and flowers, of a boat in a storm, of a tiger in a trap, of a sad lady in the palace. When the wine-merry general and rude soldiers insist that she dance with men — which no Korean virgin does, for dancing is by the sexes apart — she feels both her own modesty and her country outraged. Pretending to yield, she draws the general out of the banqueting hall down toward the river, and before he knows her purpose seizes his hands and leaps, dragging her enemy over the cliff into the other world. She died for her country: to this day the Rock of the Falling Flower is pointed out, and poets have entwined their verses around it.
summary.zh: 倭軍既敗於龜船，退而毀金石之像，掠我匠人。南方有舞伎曰龍佳者，被擄至懸崖樓，為倭將宴客起舞，素衣玉帶，妙絕一時。倭將醉，欲與之合舞；龍佳念國仇，偽諾之，引至崖畔，急挽其手，躍入深淵，同葬於水。今江畔『落花巖』即其殉國處，詩人題詠不絕。

sensitivity.note: Patriotic-legend of Nongae at Chinju's Uigok; the death scene is summarized without graphic detail.

passages.text: After the islanders in the Eastern Ocean had found out how rich Korea was, they sent a great army in a mighty fleet of ships to invade the Koreans' country. When they got to the coast they found their ships were gone: a clever Korean admiral had invented an iron-clad ship that rammed and sunk their war junks. But before the islanders left Korea they smashed statues and monuments, took marble pagodas apart to load on their ships and carry away, and enticed or forced to go with them hundreds of the Korean potters, artists, and craftsmen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Longka, the Dancing Girl' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Over three hundred years ago, when the terrible fighting dwarfs came, they encamped in a town where lived a beautiful dancing girl named Longka. Being a ge-sang, or accomplished young lady, she could sing beautifully. The islanders took this lovely damsel prisoner and made her a waitress in the general's tent. One night a great banquet was given in a famous pleasure hall named the Cliff House, built on the high bank overlooking a deep river, illuminated with a thousand wax lights, each moulded into a beautiful shape and painted with figures of flowers, birds and pet animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Longka, the Dancing Girl' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Korean dances tell stories of birds and flowers, of a boat in a storm, of a tiger in a trap, of a brave soldier in battle, or a sad lady in the palace, or of the fairy tales of the Western Queen Mother; those who know the dancer's gestures and poses, the motions of her fan and sleeves, can read the story of each told in most graceful motions. Loud was the applause among the spectators at the end of every dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Longka, the Dancing Girl' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: After the dinner was over, the general of the islanders grew very lively, and some of the rude soldiers wanted to waltz with the beautiful maiden; but it was not the custom for Korean virgins to dance with male partners, for in this Country of Gentle Manners, dancing is by the sexes apart. She thought of the thousands of her countrymen who had died in defending their beloved land. Pretending to yield to her country's enemies, she drew the general out of the banqueting hall and down toward the river, close to the edge of the rock; before he knew her purpose she seized his hands and leaped out, dragging her enemy with her over the cliff, and both passed into the other world. She died for her country. To this day the Rock of the Falling Flower is pointed out, and poets have entwined their verses around it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Longka, the Dancing Girl' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

region.en: Stony mountain valley; Star Land above (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Fairy-tale marriage from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'A Frog for a Husband', eBook #67180

summary.en: Old farmer Pak We, poor and childless, finds his pond drying and his fish gone — and in the mud a bullfrog nearly as big as an elephant, blinking at him. Instead of anger the frog bows: 'Don't worry, Farmer Pak. You'll be glad of it, by and by. I want to go home with you and live in your house.' Entertained in a room of leaves and water, the affable frog sings at dawn, and everything the old couple wished for arrives in troops — oxen, donkeys, jade and gold, a mirror like the full autumn moon, a new house like a palace. After a week the frog informs Pak he must get him a wife, and none but Miss Peach, daughter of the retired squeeze-magistrate Poom. Asked the suitor's family name, Pak is pressed until he confesses the bridegroom is a frog; the furious Poom orders him bound to the cross-bench for twenty blows — but before the first blow falls the sky darkens, lightning flashes, thunder rolls and hail pelts like cannon-balls. Mightily impressed, Poom agrees; the bride enters the palanquin with her eyes sealed in wax, Korean brides seeing nothing of their husbands until the bridal chamber. Unsealing her eyes there, she finds a frog, and in bitter disappointment seizes the scissors he offers and cuts the skin from nape to waist — out of which he twists, pulling off the speckled hide and standing a prince: fair, tall, gorgeously arrayed, with golden dragons on his shoulders and the cap of royalty. As son of the King of the Stars, condemned to live as a frog until he performed three tasks — drink up the lake, eat all the fish, and win the handsomest woman in the world — a silver chariot now appears and bears the pair beyond the clouds; from this time forth a new double star is seen in the sky.
summary.zh: 老農樸某池涸魚空，得一巨蛙。蛙曰『毋憂，攜吾歸，必有後福』。蛙夜歌，則牛馬金玉自至，屋舍煥然。一週後蛙求娶桃氏之女——桃氏乃致仕贓官也。樸某告以婿為蛙，桃公大怒，命杖之；未及施刑，雷電交作，冰雹如彈。桃公懼而允婚。新娘以蠟封目入轎，入洞房始見蛙。蛙遞剪，令剖其背皮；皮裂處，一美丈夫躍出，龍紋在肩，王冠綴鑽。自言乃星王之子，謫居為蛙，功成——飲盡湖水、食盡池魚、娶天下第一美人——三事既備，乃乘銀車與妻登天。自此天上有雙星焉。

sensitivity.note: Frog-prince / animal-bridegroom type; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Things grew worse day by day until at last there were no fish. Where once sparkled the wavelets of a pond was now an arid waste of earth and stones. There in the mud among the pebbles the farmer saw a bullfrog, nearly as big as an elephant, blinking at him with its huge round eyes. In a rage farmer Pak burst out, charging the frog with cruelty in eating up all the fish and drinking up all the water. But instead of being sorry, the bullfrog only blinked and bowed, saying, 'Don't worry, Farmer Pak. You'll be glad of it, by and by. Besides, I want to go home with you and live in your house.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Frog for a Husband' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the first rays of light appeared, Froggie was out on the porch singing a most melodious tune to the rising sun, and everything they had wished for seemed now at hand: oxen, donkeys and horses loaded with every kind of box, bale and bundle; troops of lovely girls in shining white taking beautiful things of jade, gold and silver; above all a polished metal mirror that looked like the full autumn moon. Soon, instead of oiled paper on the floors and smoky rafters, there rose a new house with elegant wide halls, furnished like a palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Frog for a Husband' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mr. Pak's full cup of joy was dashed when the Bullfrog informed him that he intended to marry, and would have no one but Miss Peach, the daughter of Poom. Asked the suitor's name, Pak was pressed so hard that at last he had to confess the suitor was not a man but a frog. 'What! do you want me to marry my daughter to a pond-croaker? Slaves, bring the cross-bench and give this wretch twenty blows.' But all this while the sky was darkening, and before the first blow was given the lightning flashed, the thunder rolled, and floods of rain and hail, first the size of an egg and then like cannon-balls, fell that threatened to overwhelm house and garden. 'Hold,' cried the frightened Mr. Poom; and mightily impressed, he at last agreed to let his daughter become the bride of the frog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Frog for a Husband' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: According to custom, the bride's eyes were sealed shut and covered with wax, for a Korean bride sees nothing of her husband until the bridal chamber. When in the bridal chamber the bride, her vision clear, looked up at the one she had married and found not a man but a frog, and was furiously angry. Gently the bridegroom begged her to rip open the skin along his back, for it was very tight; in her bitter disappointment she seized the scissors and cut from nape to waist, finding what seemed to be silk underneath the speckled skin. He twisted himself about, pulled his whole speckled hide hard with his front paws, and jumping out of his skin stood before his bride a prince: fair, tall, of superb figure, gorgeously arrayed, embroidery of golden dragons on his shoulders telling of his rank, and on his head the cap of royalty with a sparkling diamond in the center. He told the story of his life: as son of the King of the Stars he had committed some offense, in punishment for which his father condemned him to live upon the earth in the form of a frog, with three tasks to perform — to drink up all the water in the lake, to eat all the fish, and to win a human bride, the handsomest woman in the world. Scarcely had he spoken than a chariot and horses, silver bright, appeared at the door; bowing low to his foster-parents, the pair disappeared beyond the clouds, and from this time forth a new double star was seen in the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Frog for a Husband' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

region.en: Islands of the eastern sea (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Satirical etiology from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Shoes for Hats', eBook #67180

summary.en: Many centuries ago, when Korea was named the Land of Morning Splendor, the island-kingdom in the eastern sea was called the Land of the Dragon-Fly, and its people, warlike but rude, had no books or letters. Kind teachers filled with the spirit of Great Buddha crossed the sea to teach them politeness, reading, writing and the building of pagodas and temples. An envious queen of the islands sends her priests to the seashore at low tide to call on the spirits of the deep; the Salt Water Giant, his head covered with clam and oyster shells, carries the request down to the Dragon King of the World Under the Sea, and at flood tide the sea opens and His Majesty presents the two sparkling tide-jewels that govern the ebb and the flood. Landing on the southern coast, the queen fights many battles and seizes not common prisoners but painters, artists, costumers, makers of pottery, men of books and priests, carrying them to the islands, where the smart men of skill teach the islanders how to build houses and temples and be like the Koreans. Great borrowers, the islanders ask what, in time of ceremony, they should put on their heads — and the offended Koreans, in contempt, give them their old shoes with strings; the islanders put them on their heads like skull caps, tie the white strings under their chins, and to this day, when making offerings to the fairies, wear this head-gear and think their shoe-caps are very fine.
summary.zh: 東海島國遣使乞冠於朝鮮。韓人惡其侵掠工匠，乃以敝履與之。島人不識，戴之於首，以白帶繫於頷下，自以為美冠。至今其祭神之冠，猶鞋形也。

sensitivity.note: Satirical national anecdote written from a Korean-children's viewpoint; represents Sino-Korean cultural-lending debates, not fact.

passages.text: Many centuries ago when Korea was named Chosen, or the Land of Morning Splendor, the island-kingdom out in the eastern sea was called The Land of the Dragon-Fly. The Koreans called these islanders dwarfs, because they were not tall of stature, though they were very warlike and brave. The isle men had no books or letters, and were very rude in their manners; therefore many kind teachers, filled with the spirit of Great Buddha, crossed the sea from Everlasting Great Korea, to teach these islanders politeness, and how to read and write, and to build pagodas, and temples and schools.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The islanders had priests who went down by the seaside when the tide was low, and called on the spirits of the deep. The first living thing that poked its nose above the waters was the Salt Water Giant, his head all covered with clam and oyster shells, sea weed, shrimps and whatever grows in the bottom of the ocean; a grumpy sort of fellow, he carried the request down to his master, the Dragon King of the World Under the Sea. No sooner did the tide show flood than the sea opened, and His Majesty appeared in a great sea shell, holding the two sparkling tide-jewels which govern the ebb and the flood tides, which he presented to the Queen before quickly disappearing beneath the waves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Immediately after receiving the tide jewels, the Queen landed on the southern coast of Korea; she cared nothing about common prisoners, but whenever she found a painter, an artist, a costumer, a maker of pottery, or a man of books, or a priest, she seized and took him along. In the islands these smart men of skill taught the islanders how to build houses, palaces, and temples, to make fine clothes, to paint pictures — so the islands became rich in fruit, rice, grain, pagodas and temples.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Koreans were greatly offended at these savages from over the sea for invading their country and taking away their artists and craftsmen, and resolved to play a trick on the islanders. So when men from the isles sent a company of men to Korea and asked for caps to put on their heads, the Koreans in contempt gave them their old shoes, which had strings on them to tie over their feet. The islanders did not know what these shoes were, and put them on their heads like skull caps, tying them with the white strings down under their chins. So to this day the islanders, when making offerings to the fairies, wear this head-gear and think their shoe-caps are very fine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Voice of the Bell: In-Jung of Seoul

texts.period: Bell legend from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913); bell cast under King Taejo (r. 1392-1398)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Voice of the Bell', eBook #67180

summary.en: When Tai Jo, first King of the new dynasty, built Han Yang, the workmen digging for the East Gate foundations came upon a bell — a lucky omen. But such a bell could only tinkle, and the king wanted one to boom loud and long, to excel even the famed bell of Silla: ten feet high, eight feet across, crowned by two terrible dragons, hung by whole tree-trunks, struck by a swinging log instead of a clapper, its guardian spirit of the city housed in the bell. Copper and tin came in by bullock-cart and donback from every province; the pit was dug, the crucibles fired — and the casting cracked. A second casting cracked; a third cracked, until the price of a palace had been paid and there was no bell. Out steps a workman who recalls a collector's story: in a certain village an old woman carrying a baby boy strapped to her back had no coin to give but offered the child herself. The baby is thrown into the half-filled mould — the casting is perfect, and the bell is named In Jung, 'Man Decides': every night at nine o'clock every man must decide to go to bed, and until midnight the women have the streets to themselves. When first sounded, the bell discovers it has a memory and a voice: 'Mu-u-u-ma-ma-ma-la-la-la' ending like a baby's cry — 'My mother's fault. My mother's fault.' To this day the mothers in Seoul, as they clasp their darlings to their bosoms, resolve it shall be no fault of theirs if these lack love or care.
summary.zh: 太祖築漢陽城，東門掘得古鐘，以為瑞。然其聲細，乃募銅鑄巨鐘，高丈、闊八尺，頂蟠雙龍。三鑄三裂。有司言某村嫗曾願以孺子獻銅，未收。至四鑄，銅半熔，擲嬰兒入之，鐘乃成，名曰『人定』——每夜九點，男子皆歸寢，婦人始得遊於街。初鳴之日，鐘聲如嬰啼，曰『母之過也，母之過也』。都中母氏聞之，益慈其子。

sensitivity.note: Child-sacrifice-in-casting legend attached to the Jongno bell (Bosingak); handled at summary level.

passages.text: When Tai Jo, the great general and first King of Korea, founded a new dynasty, he moved the capital near the great river Han and resolved to build a mighty city called Han Yang, the Castle on the Han. Happy was he when the workmen, in digging for the foundations of the East Gate, came upon a bell: it was a lucky omen. But such a bell could only tinkle, while King Tai Jo wanted one that would boom loud and long, that would excel even the famed striker of the hours in Silla, and flood miles of hill and valley with its melody. The guardian spirit of the city would have its home in the bell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Word was sent out to all the provinces to collect the copper and tin to make the bronze metal. When there was not yet enough, one of the collectors came to a certain village and called at a house where lived an old woman carrying a baby boy strapped to her back; she had no coin, cash, metal, or fuel to give, but was quite ready to offer either herself or the baby: 'May I give you this boy?' The collector paid no attention to her, but passed on; when in Seoul, however, he told the story, and thus it came to pass that many heard of the matter and remembered it later.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the fire-clay crucibles were set on the white-hot coals and the hissing, molten stream ran out and filled the mould, alas! they found the bell cracked. A second casting was made, but again, when cool, it was found to be cracked. Three separate times this happened, until the price of a palace had been paid and yet there was no bell. King Tai Jo offered a large reward, whereupon out stepped a workman who told the story of the old woman, and said that the bell would crack after every cooling unless her proposal was accepted. So the baby boy was sent for and, when the liquid metal had half filled the pit, was thrown into the mass; when they hoisted the cooled bell up from the mould, lo, the casting was a perfect success. It was named In Jung, 'Man Decides': every night at nine o'clock let every man or boy decide to go to bed, and from that hour until midnight the women shall have the streets to themselves to walk in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: As yet the bell was silent. When it did sound, the Seoul people discovered that it was the most wonderful bell ever cast: it had a memory and a voice, it could wail as well as sing. Its sounds actually made a sentence — 'Mu-u-u-ma-ma-ma-la-la-la-la' until it ended like a baby's cry: 'My mother's fault. My mother's fault.' And to this day the mothers in Seoul, as they clasp their darlings to their bosoms, resolve that it shall be no fault of theirs if these lack love or care.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The King of the Sparrows and His Rewards

region.en: Sparrow Capital among the eaves (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Bird-reward tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The King of the Sparrows', eBook #67180

summary.en: A young sparrow, caught in the split-bamboo curtain after escaping the roof-snake, has its leg put out of joint; the kind owner of the house sets the leg in place with moist clay and feeds it till it is strong. The sparrow flies to the King of Sparrow Land, and the court votes to reward the good man richly: by magic they pack gold, jade, brocade, cups and saucers, rice, horses and oxen, pretty maids, silk and cotton clothes and things to eat into a seed. Planted, it grows a luxuriant vine with one unusually fine gourd, which when opened in autumn yields a table of costly jade, a silver bottle of wine, gold tea-caddy, rolls of silk and satin, rice and cooked foods, horses and oxen, and last of all lovely girls who serve the feast — the old couple live as happy as king and queen. A wicked man who hated all sparrows hears of it, breaks a sparrow's leg and binds it with clay and a rag until it is dreadfully crooked; the Sparrow King hands him a seed, and the vine covers all three of his thatched roofs — but the gourds, opened one by one, yield the twelve curses of Korea: rope-dancers demanding pay, begging priests, hired mourners with a corpse, dancing girls, acrobats, loafers from the government offices, fortune-tellers, jugglers, blind folks with bells, and a giant threatening to eat the pair; the twelfth gourd holds all the smells of Korea, and as they run holding their noses a gale blows the house down, the thatch bursting into flame from the flue fires. Stripped of everything, the wicked fellow and his wife live the rest of their days on their neighbor's charity.
summary.zh: 雀為屋蛇所傷，善人為之接骨。雀王賜以一籽，種之生瓜，剖之則玉桌、金瓶、錦緞、僕婢皆出，夫婦遂富。惡鄰效之，故折雀足而偽為救之，雀王亦賜一籽。瓜成十二，剖之則雜技、游僧、喪班、歌伎、衙役、瞽者、巨人絡繹而出，皆索錢；末瓜臭不可近，烈風拔屋，火焚其廬。惡人夫婦遂賴善人之施以終老。

sensitivity.note: Same gourd-reward plot family as Hungbu-Nolbu (cf. korean-hungbu-gourd-treasures).

passages.text: One day a young sparrow that had hardly learned to fly was almost seized by the roof-snake, but was saved by a big, brave bird. Although escaped from the snake's jaws, the sparrow in falling caught its legs in the curtain made of split bamboo, and its limb was put out of joint. The owner of the house was a kind man, who loved the birds: taking pity on the poor sparrow, he set its leg in place, put moist clay around the broken part, kept it warm, and fed the birdie until it was strong again, letting it fly away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: It spread its wings to fly to the King of the Sparrows, and His Majesty and his counselors voted to reward richly so good a friend of all sparrows. By some magic process they packed gold, jade, brocade, cups and saucers, rice, horses, oxen, pretty maids, silk and cotton clothes and delicious things to eat and drink into a seed, and gave it to the sparrow to carry to the good man. The wife, who was a wise woman, begged her husband to keep it, and on a warm day in spring she planted it: it grew to be a luxuriant vine, and when the gourd, fully ripe, was sawed open, lo! a store of riches came out such as neither the man nor his wife had ever dreamed of — a table of costly jade, a silver bottle of delicious wine, rolls of silk and satin, rice and cooked food, strong horses and fat oxen, and last of all some lovely young girls, as fair as the moon, who served the feast, as if they had been used to waiting on ladies and gentlemen all their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: But a wicked man that hated all sparrows heard of his neighbor's good fortune and was envious; he threw a stick at a bird and broke its leg, then bound up the limb with clay and a bit of rag, keeping the poor sparrow until its leg was well but dreadfully crooked. The Sparrow King handed out a seed to be given to the enemy of the sparrows; the naughty man planted it, and the vine covered the whole side of the house and all the thatched roofs of the three dwellings which made up his home. In the autumn he plucked the fruit and sawed them open.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Instead of good things and treasures, there came out one after another the twelve curses of Korea: a party of rope dancers who demanded money; a line of Buddhist priests begging for the temples; a band of hired mourners carrying a corpse; a bevy of dancing girls; a pair of acrobats; loafers from the government offices, fortune-tellers, jugglers, and blind folks with sticks and bells; finally a giant that threatened to eat up both the man and his wife. By this time there was not a coin left. When the twelfth gourd was opened it seemed to have in it all the smells of Korea; holding their noses, the man and his wife ran out of their house — happily, for just then a gale of wind blew down the house, and the thatch and timbers burst into flames from the fire that had heated the flues. Thus stripped of all their possessions because of the man's cruelty to the birds, the wicked fellow and his wife would have starved, except for the kindness of the good man who treated the sparrows kindly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Keel Wee and the Game with the Mountain Fairies

texts.period: Fairy-tale of Rip Van Winkle type from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies', eBook #67180

summary.en: Over half a thousand years ago the wood-cutter Keel Wee of a northern village near P'yongyang climbs the mountain to cut wood and finds two fairy-like beings in the costume of the Chow dynasty of two thousand years before, seated on stones playing go-ban. They seem by eye-winks to invite him to look on; when he stretches forth his hand to move a piece, the fairy nearest gives him a crack on the fingers, then puts in the woodman's mouth something like a persimmon seed. Hour after hour he watches, forgetting that with mountain spirits there is no night or morning — in fairy-land there is no time. Suddenly the timber of his axe turns to dust, his chin falls, and he tumbles over the checker-board. The fairies are gone; the stones are warm to his touch; his iron axe-head is rusty and half buried in the ground. He has grown a long white beard, his hat has rotted away, his joints are stiff, his hair has burst its topknot string and hangs grayish-white down his back. Hobbling into the village he is knocked flat by a glass window, nearly run over by a house on wheels that hums like a squirrel — a trolley. When the stone drops from his mouth his tongue is loosed, and a dignified gentleman answers that a wood-cutter of that name went up into the mountains five hundred years ago and was eaten by a tiger; yonder in the graveyard are buried ten or more generations of his descendants. Next morning all that is seen of Keel Wee is a mass of dust, rags, some bones and much long white hair — and around his grave spring up strange flowers that bloom only on the high mountains.
summary.zh: 平壤樵夫奇遇：入山見二仙對弈，凝神觀之。仙投桃核一枚於其口，遂忘歲月。斧柄朽而墜，鬚髮皆白。歸村則電線、玻璃、鐵車遍佈，衣冠皆非。詢其家，則五百年前其人已為虎所食，墳中子孫十餘世矣。翌日樵夫化為塵土白髮一堆，墳頭生山中異花。

sensitivity.note: Rip Van Winkle / Urashima-type tale with a modern coda; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Over a half thousand years ago there lived in a northern village, near Ping Yang, a wood-cutter named Keel Wee. Arriving in the woods at a clearing, he spied at some distance off two fairy-like beings, dressed in the costume of the Chow dynasty of two thousand years ago; they sat on stones and played the game of go-ban. Coming near, the woodman took a respectful attitude, and the two fairies seemed by eye-winks to invite him to look on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Forgetting himself and his manners, he stretched forth his right hand to move one of the pieces. At once the fairy nearest to him gave him a crack on the fingers for his impudence, and jerked his arm away; then, without saying a word, he took out from his wallet something that looked like a persimmon seed and put it in the woodman's mouth. Hour after hour the game proceeded; Keel Wee became more and more wrapped up in the game, for he had forgotten that with mountain spirits there is no night or morning, nor passing of the hours — in fairy-land there is no time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddenly the timber of his axe seemed to turn to dust and his chin fell; he tumbled over, upsetting the checker-board. When he looked up, the fairies were gone, and the stones they had used as seats were warm to his touch. He put his hand to his breast and found that he had grown a long white beard; the iron axe-head was rusty and half buried in the ground, his hat rotted away, his joints stiff, his clothes a mass of rags, and his hair had burst its topknot string and hung down his back grayish-white.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Instead of the two grinning idol posts that had stood before every Korean hamlet since the days of Kija, there was a line of high thick poles with iron wire stretching for miles; his face was flattened against something hard which he could see through, and a young man shouted, 'Here, you mountain daddy, let that glass alone.' A house on wheels came right at him on two lines of shining iron, and the conductor called, 'Hello, old goblin, where did you get your pumpkin mouth? Look out or you'll swallow the moon. Get out of the way of the trolley.' Catching sight of a dignified gentleman in flowing white clothes, Keel Wee bowed his head low; as he did so the stone put in his mouth by the fairies dropped out, and his tongue was loosed. The gentleman cried, 'Heavens! man, are you a beggar-spirit of the mountains? Your speech sounds like the dialect spoken in these parts five hundred years ago; the head of such a family, a wood-cutter, is reported to have gone up into the mountains and was eaten up by a tiger. Yonder in the graveyard are buried ten or more generations of his descendants.' Next morning, all that was seen of Keel Wee was a mass of dust, rags, some bones, and much long white hair; when they buried him, there sprang up around his grave strange flowers that bloomed only on the high mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
